title: Nature becomes a cross-party source of pride, place attachment, and electoral accountability
source_unit: More in Common with the National Trust, RSPB, WWF, Woodland Trust, and Wildlife Trusts, Strong Roots: the role of nature in uniting voter coalitions
geography: Great Britain; national survey and swing-voter focus groups

observations.period: August–September 2026; nature as shared identity and place attachment

denominator.unit: Britons surveyed in August 2026; three swing-voter focus groups supplemented the survey

nature_pride.value: Nature and green spaces are described as among the largest sources of local pride

cross_party_nature_care.value: Care for nature and wildlife extends across the political spectrum, including among people sceptical of climate action

nature_identity_mechanism.value: Nature operates as a shared place and identity resource that can cross partisan climate-policy divisions

observations.method: More in Common national survey of 2,006 Britons in August 2026 plus three focus groups of swing voters in Makerfield, Dorking and Horley, and Enfield North.
observations.uncertainty: The study is commissioned and co-produced with conservation charities; the accessible summary does not provide the full questionnaire, weighting details, or every subgroup base. Qualitative findings are not population estimates.
observations.subgroup: British voters across party groups, with qualitative work focused on swing voters.
observations.counterinterpretation: Stated care for nature may express local pride or general values without implying willingness to pay, accept restrictions, change consumption, or support a particular policy instrument.

observations.period: August–September 2026; nature, cost of living, and development are not experienced as a forced binary

nature_development_binary.value: Respondents reject the idea that protecting nature must conflict with development or attention to cost-of-living priorities

forced_tradeoff.value: When politicians force a nature-versus-development trade-off, the report says respondents side firmly with nature protection

policy_meaning.value: Nature policy is judged through both material-development concerns and a moral/place obligation to protect shared environments

observations.method: Survey questions and focus-group discussion on nature protection, development, planning, and cost-of-living priorities.
observations.uncertainty: The summary does not establish which specific development projects, costs, taxes, or local distributional effects respondents had in mind; stated trade-off preferences are not observed policy choices.
observations.subgroup: British adults and swing voters; local exposure to development, deprivation, and green-space access requires further analysis.
observations.counterinterpretation: Rejecting a binary in the abstract may not survive a concrete project with visible jobs, housing, energy, transport, or household-cost consequences.

observations.period: August–September 2026; perceived political neglect and electoral accountability

political_inaction.value: Most respondents feel politicians and political parties are not doing enough to protect wildlife and nature

government_care_gap.value: Most feel people in power care less about nature than they do

nature_accountability.value: Perceived politician positions on nature protection actively shape voter perceptions in a conjoint experiment

legitimacy_mechanism.value: Environmental protection becomes a test of whether political institutions recognize a widely shared place-based value

observations.method: National polling, focus groups, and a conjoint experiment reported by More in Common; the accessible page summarizes the direction of effects rather than publishing all estimates.
observations.uncertainty: The summary does not provide the conjoint design, effect sizes, randomization details, or realized electoral behavior; the report is not a causal estimate of vote change.
observations.subgroup: Major-party voter coalitions, including Reform, Conservative, Labour, Liberal Democrat, and Green voters.
observations.counterinterpretation: A perceived care gap may be a general anti-politician sentiment that attaches to nature, and electoral risk may depend on salience, party competition, and local context.

observations.period: August–September 2026; climate-policy identity and nature-protection coalition tension

climate_nature_split.value: Many voters connect climate change and nature, but climate-action scepticism does not eliminate strong expectations of nature protection

reform_vulnerability.value: The report identifies an electoral vulnerability when Reform UK and Nigel Farage are perceived as not caring about nature

coalition_route.value: A nature-protection coalition may be broader than a net-zero coalition, allowing cross-party environmental concern without common climate-policy ideology

observations.method: Party-segment analysis and conjoint evidence summarized in the publisher's report.
observations.uncertainty: Party-specific findings are report interpretations and do not establish stable voter realignment, policy durability, or behavior outside the survey context.
observations.subgroup: Voters aligned with the five major British parties; subgroup effects and party-specific sample sizes require the downloadable tables.
observations.counterinterpretation: Shared nature concern may fragment over net-zero policy, land use, farming, planning, water, taxation, or who bears implementation costs.

related_sources.claim: More in Common identifies downloadable polling tables for the Strong Roots report and the related August 7–10 fieldwork.
National Trust campaign page summarizes related polling on nature as a source of pride and a perceived government care gap.

boundary: This is commissioned survey and focus-group evidence about political meaning, place attachment, and environmental attitudes. It does not establish realized conservation, willingness to pay, project-level local acceptance, household affordability, emissions behavior, vote change, or policy implementation.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official More in Common Strong Roots publication page, checked for sample, methods, headline findings, nature/development framing, party-pattern interpretation, and conjoint-experiment boundary.
reproduction_audit.version_note: The accessible publisher page is a summary; full tables and the conjoint design should be consulted before making subgroup or effect-size claims.
